questions.q: You bought a non-refundable $200 concert ticket. On the night of the show you come down with a bad flu and know you'd barely enjoy the concert if you forced yourself to go — the $200 is gone either way, whether you attend or not. Many people nonetheless drag themselves to the show, reasoning 'I already paid for it, so I have to go.' What is this reasoning error called?
choices: The sunk cost fallacy — letting an unrecoverable past cost influence a decision that should be based only on future costs and benefits

questions.q: Hospital A has a higher survival rate than Hospital B for minor surgeries, and also a higher survival rate than Hospital B for major surgeries. Yet when all surgeries are combined, Hospital B has the higher OVERALL survival rate. Both sets of figures are accurate. How is this possible?
choices: It isn't possible — at least one hospital's numbers must be wrong
The combined rate is always just the average of the two category rates, so Hospital A should lead overall too
Hospital A treats a much larger share of high-risk major-surgery cases, so the riskier case mix drags down its combined rate — this is Simpson's paradox
Hospital B's doctors must simply be more skilled overall

choices: Attractive people become unpleasant because they get away with more.

questions.q: A father leaves 17 camels to his three sons: the eldest gets half, the second gets a third, and the youngest gets a ninth — numbers that don't divide 17 evenly. A wise elder lends them one camel to solve it. What happens?
choices: They now have 18 camels: the sons take 9, 6, and 2 camels respectively (17 total), and the elder takes back the borrowed camel.
The problem has no valid solution and the will is voided by the court.
The 17 camels are simply divided into three equal groups after rounding.
They now have 18 camels: the sons take 9, 6, and 3 camels respectively, and the elder keeps the borrowed camel as payment.
